entry.title: GCC String Splitting Optimization Interferes With Binary Path Audits
entry.content:
Links: stoppels.ch | lobsters | hacker news

Linux distributions and package managers frequently audit compiled binaries for non-relocatable absolute build paths using standard string searches. However, modern versions of GCC employ an optimization that splits string constants into overlapping 16-, 32-, or 64-byte pieces for vectorized move instructions, preventing these paths from appearing contiguously or at all within the compiled binary.

This compiler behavior undermines post-build audits and binary patching techniques used by tools like Conda and Spack, which rely on finding intact strings to rewrite installation prefixes. While the optimization aims to facilitate efficient SIMD memory operations, it complicates package verification and reduces binary interpretability, leaving developers with limited ways to disable the behavior short of restricting vector register widths.
